plain: The claim is that something from space hit the earth around 12,000 years ago, at the start of a sudden cold spell called the Younger Dryas, and that this impact caused the great flood remembered in old myths and wiped out an earlier human civilization. The broadcaster Joe Rogan says it on the show in his own words. Talking about a threat too big for anyone to stop, he says, "that's probably what happened during the younger dryas impact," and he connects it to ancient flood stories, among them the Epic of Gilgamesh. Michels' co-host, a defense and aerospace engineer who goes by the pseudonym Jack, mentions the same idea more briefly as "the reset 12,000 years ago". He credits it to the researcher Randall Carlson and the writer Graham Hancock and does not say what caused it. The flood tale in the Epic of Gilgamesh, in E. A. Wallis Budge's 1920 translation, is told by the flood survivor Utnapishtim: the great gods decide "to make a wind-storm," a rain-flood falls, "a black cloud from the foundation of heaven came up" with the storm god Adad thundering inside it, and the Anunnaki, whom the translator calls star-gods, "brandished their torches" and "with their glare they lighted up the land." The epic does not describe anything striking the earth. If the idea were true, human history would be much older than we think, and a catastrophe would have erased it.

discussion.by: The Epic of Gilgamish, Tablet XI (translated by E. A. Wallis Budge in The Babylonian Story of the Deluge)
discussion.text: The teller does not say which part of the epic he means; if it is the flood of the Eleventh Tablet, the source says the great gods resolved "to make a wind-storm" and tells a rain-flood, "A black cloud from the foundation of heaven came up" in which Adad thundered, while the Anunnaki, whom the translator glosses as "The star-gods of the southern sky", "brandished their torches" and "With their glare they lighted up the land". Star-gods lighting up the land with torches is the tablet's nearest image to fire from the sky; reading the flood as the memory of an impact is a step the tablet neither states nor excludes. The words are from E. A. Wallis Budge's translation (The Babylonian Story of the Deluge, 1920) of the Eleventh Tablet of the Assyrian version, in which Uta-Napishtim tells Gilgamish of the flood.
